title: 1 Chronicles 19:1–9
context: This chapter parallels 2 Samuel 10. When Nahash king of Ammon dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, but Hanun's princes accuse them of spying, and Hanun humiliates them. Knowing they have offended David, the Ammonites hire a large force of chariots and allies from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah, and David sends Joab with the army. The Chronicler's figures and place names differ in places from 2 Samuel 10, and those differences are noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: After this, Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Nahash king of Ammon dies, and his son reigns. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler places this account after David's victories in chapter 18, presenting a king whose kingdom God has established and who now deals with his neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:1. Nahash appears earlier as an enemy of Israel at Jabesh Gilead (1 Samuel 11:1), which makes David's later goodwill toward his house all the more striking.

verses.text: David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. David’s servants came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun to comfort him.
verses.arminianNotes: David resolves to "show kindness to Hanun" because Nahash showed kindness to him. Arminian readers see a sincere gesture of goodwill freely offered, which Hanun is just as free to receive or refuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Samuel 10:2 is nearly identical. Scripture does not record what kindness Nahash had shown David, and it is not supplied here; the point is David's loyal response.

verses.text: But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, “Do you think that David honors your father, in that he has sent comforters to you? Haven’t his servants come to you to search, to overthrow, and to spy out the land?”
verses.arminianNotes: Hanun's princes say David's servants have come "to search, to overthrow, and to spy out the land." Arminian readers note how suspicion, voiced by advisers, turns a gesture of comfort into a perceived threat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that bad counsel shapes Hanun's response, much as it shaped Rehoboam's (1 Kings 12). Rulers who listen to suspicious voices can turn friends into enemies.

verses.text: So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved them, and cut off their garments in the middle at their buttocks, and sent them away.
verses.arminianNotes: Hanun shaves David's servants and cuts their garments at the buttocks. Arminian readers see a deliberate act of public shame aimed at David's envoys, a choice that rejects his kindness outright.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the insult targets David through his messengers. The Chronicler records the act plainly, as 2 Samuel 10:4 does, as the decisive provocation that leads to war.

verses.text: Then some people went and told David how the men were treated. He sent to meet them; for the men were greatly humiliated. The king said, “Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”
verses.arminianNotes: David meets the humiliated men and tells them to stay at Jericho until their beards grow. Arminian readers note David's care for his servants, protecting their dignity before they return to public life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 10:5 has the same instruction. A king's concern for his humiliated servants reflects the shepherd heart that God desires in Israel's rulers.

verses.text: When the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent one thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, out of Aram-maacah, and out of Zobah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ammon sends a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. Arminian readers note that Ammon chooses escalation rather than seeking peace after offending David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Samuel 10:6 names the hired allies differently and gives no silver amount. Both texts are allowed to speak in their own words without resolving the differences.

verses.text: So they hired for themselves thirty-two thousand chariots, and the king of Maacah with his people, who came and encamped near Medeba. The children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle.
verses.arminianNotes: They hire thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maacah, encamping near Medeba. Arminian readers note the size of the coalition, showing how seriously Ammon prepared for war against Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 10:6 speaks of twenty thousand footmen, a thousand men with the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men of Tob. The figures and units differ and are noted, not harmonized.

verses.text: When David heard of it, he sent Joab with all the army of the mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: David sends Joab "with all the army of the mighty men." Arminian readers note that David responds decisively to the threat, sending his best forces under his experienced commander.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:7. The Chronicler presents David as the king who leads Israel's defense, through his commander, against nations who rise against God's people.

verses.text: The children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array at the gate of the city; and the kings who had come were by themselves in the field.
verses.arminianNotes: The Ammonites array at the city gate while the hired kings stand in the field. Arminian readers note the tactical setting that places Israel between two forces, setting up the dilemma Joab faces next.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Samuel 10:8. The arrangement creates real danger for Israel's army, so that the outcome of the battle will depend on more than human strategy.
